newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: March budget critical for S.African stocks - fund.
newsitem.headline: March budget critical for S.African stocks - fund.

text.p: South African Finance Minister Trevor Manuel's March budget will determine the performance of the Johannesburg Stock Exchange next year, Old Mutual Unit Trusts senior portfolio manager Adrian Allardice said on Monday.

"The broad All Share Index is poised to show similar gains to the past year, but the key factor for the market will be the budget, with investors seeking signs of strict controls on government spending," he said in a 1997 preview.
"The new finance minister needs to establish his credibility by cutting the deficit and the government as a whole needs to begin implementing the GEAR growth proposals," he said.

GEAR is Manuel's June 14 strategy for Growth, Employment and Redistribution, which calls for fiscal discipline, wage and price restraint and industrial incentives to push economic growth to six percent by the turn of the century.
Manuel has undertaken to cut the budget deficit to four percent of GDP in fiscal 1997/98, down from an estimated 5.1 percent in the current financial year.
Allardice said Manuel's first budget would send a signal to the market about how President Nelson Mandela's government was likely to manage the economy in the longer term.

He said unit trust fund managers were likely to retain strong rand-hedge holdings during 1997, but would already be looking towards 1998, when he said growth was likely to pick up again if Manuel's budget found favour.
"While growth is forecast to slow to two percent in 1997, 1998 should see a resumption of the upward trend provided the authorities exercise strict discipline on state expenditure," he said.
Allardice said the economy had held up well in the face of pressures in 1997 including the dramatic fall in the value of the rand.
He said consumer blue chip shares were beginning to show signs of recovery from falls this year, though their performance could be influenced by interest rates.
"Spending has continued to exert pressure on interest rates and until credit growth slows, monetary policy will remain tight," he said.
